attributes.description: Entry point for Cloud Audit Dashboards. KPIs, volume, actor risk and the live signal feed.

params.markdown:
### See who did what across your Elastic Cloud projects

This overview shows how much activity there was, who was busiest, which identities carry the most risk, and the latest events as they arrive.

Start here for a routine review or when something looks wrong, then use the links above to go deeper on one person, sign-ins, Kibana objects, data access, security or location.

**How to use it:** choose a Project, Person (email) or Client IP in the controls to focus every panel, and set the period in the time picker.

embeddableConfig.description: Total audited events over time, split by originating service. Elasticsearch audits every transport action, so its volume usually far exceeds Kibana’s — and the Kibana slice is where most of the forensic value is. The plot spans exactly the time range. The range ends a minute ago, part-way through the last bucket, so the last bar covers only part of its interval and is usually short; a bucket with no bar had no audit events delivered for it (the stream arrives in batches). Signal vs noise draws the same buckets over the same span.
embeddableConfig.title: Audit volume by source · all traffic

params.markdown:
### How to read this suite

**Routine traffic is left out** unless a panel title says *all traffic*. That covers health checks, the background requests behind each search and page load, API key lookups, bulk sign-in records, and these dashboards' own activity.

**Each identity is named** by its email address, or the API key's name when there is no email, or a numeric user ID as a last resort.

**Cloud API keys have no name** in the audit log, so they appear by the start of their ID, such as `_4KEO… · Cloud API key`.

**Locations use the real client address,** not Elastic's own network hops. *Use the information control beside a panel title for details.*

embeddableConfig.description: The top 12 identities by signal volume (fewer on a narrow screen, down to 8), in one block per kind; the rest of each kind is folded into one grey “+N more” tile (just “+N” where the tile is narrow; hover it for the count). Blocks: named API key (labelled by the KEY, with its owner — the principal that created it — on a further line when there is room, and in the tooltip); person (a real email address); cloud API key (an organization-level Cloud key, which the audit stream records only by id and with no owner); platform (Elastic’s own service accounts and automation, such as elastic/kibana, the Kibana service account); user, no email (a user name that signed in but carries no email; absent on most projects); and unattributed (no authenticated principal: <anonymous>, an unauthenticated token, or a user name that only ever failed to sign in, such as elastic or admin in a password-guessing run). An identity is one tile even when its events disagree about its kind; it goes in the most specific block any of them supports. Area grows with the SQUARE ROOT of event volume, so one dominant identity cannot crush the rest into slivers, plus the same small share for every tile, so the quietest identity keeps a readable name but is never drawn larger than a busier one. Each tile prints its event count where it fits (a bare number on a narrow tile): read the number, not the area, for how much more one identity did. A name too long for its tile ends in “…” — the tooltip has the full name and exact counts. Color is Risk total, the quantity the Security Anomalies risk leaderboard ranks by: each scoring event’s risk weight (from 10 for a workflow run to 50 for a security configuration change; 0 for anything that does not score, and 0 for Kibana’s own routine API-key clean-up, which Privileged ops leaves out too) summed over the identity’s events, on a square-root scale. It is in weight × events, not events, so it runs well above the counts on the tiles. A key that carries its creator’s email is its own tile here, but counts under the person in Busiest identities. The range ends a minute ago, so nothing in it is still arriving; each panel reads the clock for itself, up to a second apart, so two panels side by side can differ by the events of that second at either end of the range: usually none, a few on a busy all-traffic count or during a burst. That is how a tile here and the same identity’s row in Busiest identities can differ by one or two events.
embeddableConfig.title: Actor footprint · area by the square root of events, color by risk total

embeddableConfig.description: The identities generating the most signal traffic, and how varied their behaviour is; the rows sum to Signal events when they all fit, and fewer rows than the bound means every identity with signal is listed (Distinct actors counts the same set). Identity resolves to an email, then an API key name, then a user id. An identity’s treemap tile and its row here can differ by an event or two at the range’s edges, because each panel reads the clock for itself. Elasticsearch stamps an API key’s CREATOR’s email on every event the key emits, so any number of machines authenticating with one key resolve to one person: such a row reads “email · via key name” and is a credential’s traffic, not the person at a keyboard. To follow one person across the suite, pick them in the Person (email) control above. An Identity shown as “_4KEO… · Cloud API key” is an organization-level Elastic Cloud API key: the audit stream records it only by its opaque 20-character id, shown here by its first five characters; it has no name and no owner email.
embeddableConfig.title: Busiest identities · top 12 at most

embeddableConfig.description: ECS event categories over the whole stream, noise included, each with its count, on a log scale so the small categories are as readable as the bulk: read each bar by its count, not its length (each axis step is ten times the one before). event.category is a multi-value array, so an event in two categories counts once in each and the bars sum to more than the event total; “none recorded” is events that carry no category. A category with a single event has no visible bar.

embeddableConfig.description: The newest 200 signal events, newest first, behind the same noise gate as Signal events, without Kibana’s own routine API-key clean-up (invalidate_apikeys by the elastic/kibana service account, every few seconds), which would otherwise fill it: Privileged ops counts those in its “excl. N cleanups” line, and they still count in Signal events. Detail is the Kibana message, the transport action on an Elasticsearch event, or for a security change (API key, role) what it changed: “API key <name or id> + N more” for one call that invalidated several keys. A Client IP marked internal is Kibana or the platform calling Elasticsearch on someone’s behalf, not where they are; “none recorded” is an event with no client address, such as Kibana’s own service account working inside the platform. Automation reads as long runs of near-identical rows from one identity: this suite’s own install is left out by the gate, but any other script — a deploy, a scan, a tool polling an API — can fill this feed for minutes. To read past it, pick a Person above, or open the session and filter that identity out. Open the Discover session to page further back or add columns. An Identity shown as “_4KEO… · Cloud API key” is an organization-level Elastic Cloud API key: the audit stream records it only by its opaque 20-character id, shown here by its first five characters; it has no name and no owner email.
embeddableConfig.title: Live signal feed · Kibana key clean-up left out
